analysis.investment_thesis: EIH's Oberoi brand commands genuine luxury pricing power — 38.9% operating margins and 23.4% ROCE are extraordinary for an asset-heavy hotel business. At 26.5x P/E with modest 5.7% revenue CAGR over 9 years, the stock is fairly priced for what it is: an excellent business, not a compounding machine.
key_strengths: Oberoi brand moat: 38.9% operating margin and 66% gross margin reflect genuine pricing power in ultra-luxury segment
Pristine balance sheet: net cash position (cash 378 Cr > debt 265 Cr), D/E of 0.05, finance costs fell from 56 Cr (2020) to 21 Cr (2025)
Earnings leverage is real: EBITDA went from 48 Cr (FY22) to 1,298 Cr (FY25) on modest revenue recovery — margins structurally improved
key_risks: Cyclicality is brutal: revenue cratered 69% in FY21, OCF went deeply negative — Oberoi is not a recession-resistant business
Capex surge: FY25 capex hit 485 Cr (up from 138 Cr in FY23), FCF/Net Income collapsed to 45% — capital intensity is rising again
Modest long-term growth: 9-year revenue CAGR of only 5.7% and the business requires continuous heavy reinvestment to grow
red_flags: FY25 FCF of 346 Cr vs Net Income of 770 Cr (45% conversion) — well below Munger's 80% quality threshold; CWIP jumped to 403 Cr signaling major capital commitments ahead
Promoter stake at only 32.85% is low for a family-controlled luxury brand — raises questions about long-term stewardship alignment
analysis.detailed_analysis:
EIH is the operator of the Oberoi and Trident hotel brands, and the Oberoi name is genuinely among the world's elite luxury hospitality franchises. The financial evidence of pricing power is compelling: 66% gross margins and 38.9% operating margins are exceptional for a hotel operator anywhere in the world. ROCE of 23.4% clears Munger's 20% hurdle, and the near-elimination of debt (from 647 Cr in FY20 to a net cash position in FY25) reflects disciplined capital management. The FY22–FY25 recovery demonstrated strong operating leverage — EBITDA grew 27x from near-zero while revenues only grew 2.8x.

Applying Munger's inversion: what makes this a bad investment? First, hotels are inherently cyclical and asset-heavy — COVID didn't just dent earnings, it obliterated them (net loss of 375 Cr in FY21). Second, the FY25 capex jump to 485 Cr with CWIP at 403 Cr suggests a major expansion cycle that will consume cash for years. FCF/NI of 45% in FY25 is a red flag — earnings look better than they are. Third, at 17.86x EV/EBITDA and 26.5x P/E, the market already prices in the quality. The 9-year revenue CAGR of 5.7% is unimpressive for a business commanding this multiple. This is a fair price for a great brand, not a great price for a compounding machine. HOLD for existing holders; wait for a cyclical pullback to buy.
